name: Eye contact practice

lead: Eye contact practice means training yourself to hold someone's gaze during conversation so you seem more present, assured and engaged. Eye contact is a well-described form of nonverbal communication, studied as oculesics.

The chain is training a steady gaze, seeming more engaged and assured, then leaving a more confident impression. Wikipedia reports that eye contact can signal interest, forms part of flirting, and is linked in some contexts to confidence and respect, while norms differ widely between cultures. Published research on structured eye contact training is limited.

paras: People rehearse holding gaze in everyday conversation, often starting with shorter holds and breaking away naturally, or practising with a friend or mirror. It is typically built up over weeks of ordinary interactions.
Prolonged unbroken eye contact can feel overbearing, and people with autism or social anxiety may find it distressing. Cultural norms differ on how much is appropriate.

angle.text: Users practise holding eye contact so they appear more confident, engaged and present in conversation. Eye contact is well described as nonverbal communication, and norms vary across cultures.

lead: Eye contact practice means deliberately training oneself to hold another person's gaze in conversation, usually so as to come across as more confident, engaged and approachable. Eye contact, when two people look at each other's eyes at the same time, is a form of nonverbal communication studied under the heading of oculesics [1]. People who practise it treat it as part of presenting themselves well, a habit that affects how their face and expression read to others, not a change to the face itself.

Wikipedia reports that eye contact can signal interest and forms part of flirting, and that in the United States it is associated with respect, attentiveness, honesty and trustworthiness [1]. The article on oculesics links eye contact with perceived sincerity, self-confidence and credibility [1]. Norms differ widely between cultures, and people with social anxiety or autism spectrum conditions may find sustained eye contact uncomfortable.

Research on gaze is substantial, covering how people perceive and follow gaze and how the brain processes eyes as a core part of social cognition [2][2]. Published studies of structured eye-contact practice as a self-improvement method are not available.
infobox: Gaze cueing, social anxiety, autism spectrum conditions [2]

paras: Brief glances can develop into repeated eye contact that signals attraction, while unbroken staring can feel overbearing in many cultures. In crowds strangers often avoid eye contact as civil inattention. Oculesics covers eye movement, blinking, pupil dilation and gaze direction as well as eye contact [1].

Some theorists state that constant eye contact between two people is physically and mentally uncomfortable [1]. A study of 20 five-year-olds summarised on Wikipedia found that children who looked away while thinking were more likely to answer correctly, suggesting that faces can be mentally demanding to look at.

In East Asia and Nigeria, not looking directly at a person of higher status can be respectful, whereas in Western cultures averted eyes may be read as evasive. Wikipedia's oculesics article reports that Anglo-Saxons tend to hold steady eye contact while Latinos make brief contact, citing sociologist Cruz (2001), and that lowering the eyes is taught as respect toward authority in many Western Pacific, East Asian and North African cultures [1].

People with autism spectrum disorders or social anxiety may find eye contact unsettling. Social anxiety disorder is described as involving avoidance behaviours, which can include avoiding eye contact. A 2017 qualitative study of 92 autistic adults found that many hide autistic traits to fit in, and that this masking is tiring [2].

No studies found on eye contact practice as a self-improvement method for appearance. Related research includes a 2007 Psychological Bulletin review of gaze cueing and joint attention [2], a 2009 review of the neural bases of eye and gaze processing as a core of social cognition [2], and a 2011 review of evolutionary research on facial attractiveness [2].
